In 1940, a scientist hid two Nobel Prizes by dissolving them in acid.
The Nazis were invading Denmark, and two gold Nobel medals were hidden at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen.
They belonged to German physicists who opposed the Nazis. Their names were engraved on the gold.
So chemist George de Hevesy dropped them into aqua regia, an acid that dissolves gold.
He left the orange jar on a shelf.
Soldiers searched the building, and walked right past it.
After the war, he pulled the gold back out, and the medals were recast and returned to their owners.
And Hevesy later won a Nobel Prize of his own.
